title: The magi (Matthew 2:1–12)
hookLine: stargazers from the east follow a light and kneel before a toddler

lines: WHERE IS HE THAT IS BORN KING?
cards: Jerusalem, a king's court, and visitors nobody expected. Matthew says they came from the east: men who read the night sky for meaning. Far away they saw something they couldn't ignore, and they set out.
Matthew doesn't say how long the road was, or how many walked it.
Only that they came, and that in the capital they asked a dangerous question out loud: "Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him."
The king on the throne is Herod.

teach.h: NO NUMBER, NO CROWNS, NO NAMES.
teach.b: Matthew calls them magoi, and never says how many. Three is a later guess, from the three gifts. He never calls them kings either; that came later, from psalms about kings bringing gifts.
The names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar come from later legend.
Magoi meant something like wise men or astrologers: learned stargazers, perhaps from Persia or Babylon, though Matthew says only the east, and outsiders to Israel's faith.
Herod is troubled, Matthew says, and all Jerusalem with him. The chief priests and scribes look it up: the prophet Micah points to Bethlehem.

Herod sends the visitors on and asks them to come back and tell him where the child is, so he can worship too. He doesn't mean it. The star goes before them, and when it stops, "they rejoiced with exceeding great joy."
Matthew piles up the words. They find the child with Mary his mother, in a house, and they kneel.
Then they open their treasures: "gold, and frankincense, and myrrh." An old Christian reading takes them as gold for a king, incense for God, myrrh for a death to come.
Then, warned in a dream, they go home another way.

teach.h: THEY REJOICED WITH EXCEEDING GREAT JOY.
teach.b: Notice: the first people in Matthew's Gospel to worship Jesus are foreigners, following the light they had, a star, not a scripture. Western churches remember them at Epiphany, the feast of the light shown to the nations.

how: Western churches celebrate the magi at Epiphany on January 6, and in many countries children mark it with processions, sweets or chalked blessings over doorways. In Orthodox churches January 6 centers on the baptism of Jesus, and the magi are remembered at Christmas.

o: stargazers from the east who followed a star
three kings who rode camels from distant lands
court magicians in the service of King Herod

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: stargazers, learned men of the east
troubled, and all Jerusalem with him
a gift read as pointing to his death

s: Matthew says there were three wise men
he never gives a number. three was guessed later from the three gifts.
the magi found the child in a house
Matthew says they came into the house and saw the young child with Mary his mother.
the Bible names them Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar
those names come from legends written centuries later.

games.q: you're the magi. you've found the child, and King Herod asked you to come back and tell him where he is. then you have a dream. what do you do?
o: go back to Herod, as he asked.
stay in Bethlehem to guard the child.
games.why: warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.

practice: Ask what has been pulling at your attention lately: not a duty but a curiosity, a question you keep coming back to, a book you keep meaning to open, a person you'd like to know better, a place you keep wondering about.
Don't judge whether it's important; the magi followed a light in the sky, so just find yours and look at it for a while. If you pray, you can ask where it leads.

wordCard.voice: The magi. Stargazers from the east, no number given, who followed a light and knelt before a child. Our word magic comes from the same root.

orig.note: Greek: magi, learned stargazers, perhaps from Persia or Babylon. Magic comes from the same root.

carryVoice: Your line: follow the star you have. Tomorrow, the road turns dark. See you then.
